title: The sensor is the frame buffer: pixel charge held for on-demand readout
idea: Constraint (printable/roll-to-roll): a large-area printed oxide-TFT backplane, like those in flat-panel X-ray detectors, integrates each frame and holds it as pixel charge for tens of milliseconds. The host reads out only the regions it wants; pixels it never requests are never digitized or written to DRAM.
why: Removes the ingest frame buffer in high-resolution scanners and in document, industrial and X-ray imaging; DRAM per channel drops ~5-20x.

title: Per-application trained zstd dictionaries in kernel memory compression
idea: Inverts 'one generic compressor fits all memory': zswap/zram trains a zstd dictionary per workload class (Java heap, Python objects, protobufs) from sampled cold pages and recompresses cold pages with it on idle cores. Software on existing servers.
why: Dictionaries lift compression on small pages from ~2.5x to ~4x, freeing another 10-20% of DRAM fleet-wide.

title: KV cache kept as tokens; idle tensor cores recompute it
idea: IFR: the KV cache costs zero bytes. Closest achievable: store only token IDs plus a residual-stream checkpoint every 8th layer; during memory-bound decode the otherwise idle tensor cores re-derive K/V for the seven intervening layers block by block, overlapped with the weight fetch.
why: Attacks HBM capacity and the HBM TSV tax (facts 5, 6): KV footprint down ~6-8x for ~15-25% extra FLOPs that decode leaves unused anyway.

title: Farmer's almanac: seasonal working-set forecasts drive safe memory overcommit
idea: Farmers plant by the almanac. A controller learns each VM or pod's daily and weekly working-set seasonality from sampled PTE access bits and overcommits hosts to the forecast plus a margin. A zswap/CXL compressed tier acts as the 'frost guard' that absorbs mispredictions. It ships as open-source KVM and Kubernetes plugins with a 3-person team within $1M.
why: Allocated memory averages 40-60% utilization. Forecast-based overcommit reaches 1.3-1.6x effective capacity per DIMM.

title: Memory ballooning, fixed: controller-tracked zero lines for instant overcommit
idea: Balloon drivers fail in practice: slow, guest-cooperative and prone to thrash. The memory controller tracks all-zero and guest-hinted free lines in a bitmap, returns backing frames to the hypervisor instantly, and materializes zeros on read, so overcommit no longer depends on guest drivers.
why: Enables safe 1.3-1.5x VM overcommit, cutting DRAM per host.

title: Silicon-carbide gain-cell scratchpad holds activations refresh-free at 125 C
idea: Build the NPU's activation scratchpad from 2T gain cells in 4H-SiC. The 3.26 eV bandgap keeps generation leakage below ~1e-21 A even at 125 C, which gives retention of minutes, so whole-layer activations stay on-die instead of spilling to external DRAM.
why: External DRAM for activations disappears from hot edge and automotive NPUs. The cells need no refresh at temperatures where DRAM needs 4x refresh.

title: Recompute beats retain: drop KV between turns, then re-prefill
idea: Inverts 'prefill is expensive and KV is cheap': at 4x DRAM prices, holding a user's KV through human think time costs more per GB-hour than the prefill FLOPs to rebuild it. The server keeps only token text between turns, re-prefills on existing GPUs, and a cost model picks keep, spill or recompute per session.
why: Idle sessions are typically >90% of open sessions, so resident KV drops several-fold for chat fleets, in software only.

title: Cold-byte reaper right-sizes heaps using idle-page tracking
idea: Inverts 'allocated means needed': page-idle tracking (DAMON or the idle bitmap) finds heap regions untouched for minutes, and an agent then lowers JVM -Xmx, Go GOMEMLIMIT and cache sizes per service, rolling back on latency regressions. Software only.
why: Fleet audits typically find 20-40% of resident memory cold; right-sizing frees that DRAM in servers already installed.

title: Swap generic LZ4 page compression for per-app trained dictionaries
idea: Substitute a one-size codec with app-specific dictionaries. zswap/zram trains a zstd dictionary per cgroup from sampled pages (repeated object headers, layouts, strings), compresses that app's cold pages with it, and retrains nightly. It is a kernel-only change.
why: Raises cold anonymous-memory compression from ~2.5x to ~4-5x, so the same DIMMs hold 30-50% more working set.

title: Pheromone-trail hash marks let tenants converge on shared pages
idea: A CXL switch keeps a decaying 'pheromone' table of content hashes recently written by any VM; when another tenant writes a page whose hash hits a strong trail, the switch maps it copy-on-write to the existing physical page. Trails evaporate, so only popular content (OS images, model weights, libraries) is deduplicated, without full memory scans.
why: Multi-tenant capacity: 15-40% dedup across VMs and inference replicas at negligible scan cost.

title: Minify ECC overhead by compressing lines to embed ECC
idea: Minify the ECC chip overhead: each 64 B line is compressed just enough to hold its own ECC bits inline, so the DIMM drops its 9th or 10th ECC device. The rare incompressible line spills to a small overflow region.
why: Recovers the 12.5-25% of DRAM bits now spent on ECC devices at near-equal reliability.

title: Flight-recorder templates: logs stored as template IDs plus variables
idea: From flight data recorders that encode events compactly: logging libraries and memory-resident log stores split each line into a static template (stored once, given an ID at compile time) and typed variable fields packed columnar in binary, never materializing text.
why: Log text is 10-50x redundant; template encoding cuts in-memory log and trace buffers 10x+, with matching fab-water savings.

title: Page-aligned pruning plus copy-on-write zero page
idea: Combine the OS shared zero frame with structured sparsity: train or prune so whole 4-64 KB weight/activation blocks are exactly zero, then map those virtual pages to one physical zero frame; the GPU/CPU MMU flags them so reads return zeros without touching DRAM.
why: 30-60% block-sparse models shrink physically with no new tensor format or kernels, and bandwidth to zero pages disappears too.

title: Seed-bank keeper: pages stored as generator plus seed
idea: A seed bank stores seeds, not forests. A userfaultfd library lets programs register regions produced by deterministic generators (PRNG noise, dropout masks, random projections, synthetic test data, procedurally initialized tensors) as (generator ID, seed, offset). Under pressure the pages are dropped, and on a fault they are regenerated bit-exactly with vectorized Philox at >10 GB/s.
why: Random data defeats every compressor yet has near-zero Kolmogorov size. This frees tens of GB per training or simulation node for about $300k of engineering.

title: Reference-only reading room: back-end ReRAM layer holds model weights
idea: Reference books are read but never checked out: deposit HfOx/TaOx ReRAM crossbars (<=400 C) in the accelerator's upper metal stack to hold inference weights written once per deployment (needing only ~1e3-1e4 endurance), leaving DRAM/HBM for KV and activations only.
why: Weights are 40-70% of inference HBM; monolithic back-end storage frees that capacity while sidestepping the unlimited-endurance requirement that killed ReRAM as DRAM.

title: Planet-once pages: content-addressed dedup inside the CXL memory switch
idea: Po: every byte exists only once on Earth. The rack's CXL switch hashes each 4 KB page written to pooled memory and maps identical pages (OS images, container layers, libraries, shared model weights, zero pages) to one physical copy with copy-on-write, across all hosts rather than inside one hypervisor as KSM does.
why: Cross-host duplication in VM/container fleets is 15-40%; switch-level dedup recovers most of it with no per-host CPU scanning.

title: Mott-oscillator phase locking flags duplicate pages for inline dedup
idea: Each page fingerprint drives a row of NbO2 threshold-switch relaxation oscillators through bit-weighted coupling resistors. Rows fed identical patterns injection-lock in phase within ~100 cycles, while different patterns stay incoherent. One phase detector therefore answers 'does this page duplicate any of N stored signatures?' in parallel, and a hit triggers copy-on-write page merging in the hypervisor.
why: Dedup across VMs and containers saves 15-40% of DRAM in cloud hosts. The all-to-all compare costs O(1) energy instead of hashing and searching on every write.

title: NbO2 Mott spiking encoders store activations as sparse events
idea: NbO2 Mott threshold-switch oscillators convert layer activations into spike trains. The insulator-metal transition sits near 800 C, so devices stay stable at 125 C ambient. Only spike addresses (typically 5-10% density) are written to memory as event lists, not dense tensors.
why: Activation memory drops 10-20x for sensor-processing networks.

title: Flour sifter: multi-sieve sketches replace exact tables, median rejects flips
idea: Millers sift flour through a stack of sieves. Exact counting and lookup tables (flow tables, feature-frequency counters, dedup indices, recommendation counts) are replaced by count-median sketches with 5 'sieves' of saturating 8-bit log counters. Taking the median across sieves rejects a counter that a flip pushed up or down, so 1% BER barely moves the estimate.
why: Sketches use 10-100x less memory than exact hash tables at bounded error, and the median turns 1% cell BER into a negligible error.

title: Rack-wide content-hash page fabric: one physical copy per rack
idea: Inverts 'memory is private to each host': a CXL 3.x switch keeps a hash-indexed page directory so identical 4 KB pages (OS images, shared libraries, model weights, zero pages) across every server in a rack map to one physical copy in a pooled tier, with copy-on-write on store. Hashing runs in the switch ASIC at line rate, so no host CPU scans pages as per-host KSM does.
why: Capacity: cloud VM fleets show 20-40% cross-VM duplicate pages, and inference fleets holding identical weights collapse N replicas to ~1 per rack, so DRAM per rack drops 1.3-3x.

title: Layer-stride KV checkpoints recomputed by idle tensor cores
idea: TRIZ #8 Counterweight: balance scarce memory with abundant FLOPs by storing the residual-stream hidden state only every Nth layer (e.g., N=4) for cold tokens and recomputing the intermediate layers' K/V on demand during decode, using the tensor-core slack that memory-bound decode leaves idle.
why: Decode runs at 10-30% compute utilization; spending that slack cuts cold-context KV memory ~3-4x with modest added latency.

title: Ever-read bits drive automatic right-sizing of oversized buffers
idea: A byte that is written but never read delivers zero information. The memory controller keeps an ever-read bit per cache line, cleared on allocation; the allocator periodically scans and shrinks ring buffers, caches and pools whose tails are never read, and profilers report never-read bytes to developers.
why: Oversized buffers and caches commonly waste 10-30% of a service's footprint, and telemetry-driven trimming recovers most of it.

title: Game texture artist: store tensors in GPU texture compression formats
idea: Game artists have shipped fixed-rate block-compressed textures (BC/ASTC) for decades, and GPU texture units decode them for free. Weights and cached activations are packed as 4x4 blocks in an ASTC-like fixed-rate tensor format and read through the otherwise idle texture-sampling path, which decompresses at line rate with random access and no indirection tables.
why: This gives a fixed 3-6x compression with random access and no ALU cost, using silicon already on every GPU. HBM capacity and bandwidth per model shrink by the same factor.

title: Swap stored embedding rows for IDs hashed through a tiny MLP
idea: Substitute lookup with generation. Recommendation models replace multi-TB ID embedding tables with deep hash embeddings: k hash functions turn each ID into a dense code, a small shared MLP produces the embedding on the fly, and exact rows are kept only for the hottest 1% of IDs.
why: Embedding tables dominate recommendation DRAM, and generating rows cuts them 10-100x at small accuracy cost on unchanged servers.

title: Bytes-per-feature regression gate in CI
idea: Worsen: hide memory cost from developers so bloat compounds every release. Flip: CI measures resident bytes per feature on reference workloads, prices them at live DRAM cost, and blocks merges that add memory without a signed budget increase.
why: Capacity: cultural and tooling lever that historically recovers 20-50% of footprint over a few release cycles.

title: Lead's RoHS precedent: binding memory-energy labels for AI services
idea: As RoHS pushed lead out of electronics, a JEDEC/OCP standard backed by federal procurement requires every AI deployment and accelerator to publish measured DRAM picojoules per token and resident bytes per user, with procurement thresholds that tighten to 10x lower memory energy per access over five years.
why: A binding, measurable target pushes vendors toward on-chip reuse, compression and sparsity, makes energy per memory access a competitive metric, and slows DRAM demand growth by the same factor (energy, policy).

title: Swap regional peak provisioning for follow-the-sun memory-heavy scheduling
idea: Substitute local peaks with a global flat curve. Memory-hungry, latency-tolerant jobs (batch analytics, embedding builds, offline inference, evals) are checkpointed and moved to regions in their local night, when interactive services leave DRAM idle.
why: Diurnal swings leave 30-40% of DRAM idle at night. Filling those troughs lets fleets buy ~15-25% less DRAM for the same work, with no hardware change.

title: Compression-funded inline ECC eliminates the dedicated ECC chips
idea: Combine lossless cache-line compression (base-delta / frequent-pattern) with error correction: any 64 B line that compresses by at least 8 B stores its own strong ECC in the freed bits, so the 9th/10th ECC DRAM device on each server rank is dropped. Rare incompressible lines spill to a small overflow region flagged by a pointer bit.
why: Removes the 12.5-25% of DRAM bits that servers spend on ECC devices while keeping chipkill-class protection.

title: Helium leak test for heaps: tracer-tagged allocations expose bloat
idea: Borrowing the industrial helium leak test, the allocator stamps each allocation with a 12-bit call-site tracer in spare pointer/tag bits (MTE-style), and a memory-controller sniffer samples which tracer IDs are written but never re-read for N minutes. The fleet-wide profile auto-shrinks caches, caps pools and frees leaked objects at those call sites.
why: Production heaps carry 20-40% never-reused or leaked bytes; finding them by call site with hardware sampling instead of heap dumps recovers ~15-25% DRAM per service at negligible overhead (cost/bit).

title: Carbon antifuse ROM executes OS and library code in place
idea: IFR: immutable software consumes no RAM. Closest with C, H, Al and Si only: a one-time-programmable crossbar where a-C:H films between Al lines are fused into sp2 filaments by current pulses; each OS release, runtime and standard library is burned once and mapped execute-in-place, so code pages never occupy DRAM.
why: Code and read-only data are 5-15% of RSS on servers and phones; removed from DRAM for pennies of carbon.

title: Speculative decoding lets big models live in host DRAM, not HBM
idea: Box: amortize × decode algorithm × k-token draft window × per step × target weights in installed host DDR. A small draft model in HBM proposes k tokens and the large model verifies them in one pass, so each large-model weight read is amortized over k×batch tokens and its weights can sit in slower, already-installed host memory.
why: Cuts HBM needed per served model 3–5× by tolerating lower weight bandwidth; algorithm-only on existing servers, so no new fluorinated chemistry.

title: Three-life DIMMs: cascade U.S.-made modules from AI to edge
idea: Po: the same 42 mg of silicon is sold three times. U.S.-made modules are leased with take-back: first life in AI servers, then re-tested and re-binned (speed, ECC margin, row-hammer threshold) in U.S. facilities for web tiers, then remounted on CXL cards for cold-tier and edge use, stretching service life from ~5 to ~10-12 years.
why: Roughly halves new-DRAM demand per unit of deployed capacity over a decade and keeps scarce domestic bits in service.

title: Eliminate per-pod JVM headroom with a node-level elastic heap broker
idea: A sidecar daemon watches GC pressure across all JVMs on a node and, through GC tuning hooks and madvise, shrinks idle heaps and lends the freed pages to busy ones in real time, instead of each pod reserving its own peak.
why: Kubernetes Java fleets overprovision heap 1.5-3x; pooling headroom per node saves 25-40% of DRAM.

title: Android lifecycle for servers: killable services with saved state bundles
idea: Like Android killing background apps after they save an instance-state bundle, a server framework requires each service to serialize its minimal semantic state (not its heap) to persistent memory on a trim signal, so the OS can kill idle services aggressively and rehydrate them later.
why: Semantic state is often 100-1000x smaller than the heap; reclaims DRAM from idle microservices and makes their state power-safe.

title: RAID for RAM: erasure-coded stripes replace triple-copy replicas
idea: Distributed in-memory stores (Redis replicas, parameter servers, failover KV-cache copies) keep 2-3 full copies; instead stripe data with Reed-Solomon (e.g. 8+2) across nodes' DRAM over RDMA/CXL and reconstruct on node loss as RAID-6 does for disks.
why: Cuts redundancy overhead from 200% to 25%, ~2.4x less DRAM for fault-tolerant in-memory tiers.

title: Nitrogen triple bond broken: erasure-coded RAM replaces 3x replication
idea: N2's triple bond is strength bought with waste; in-memory databases and caches that keep three full replicas instead stripe objects as (k=10, m=2) Reed-Solomon fragments across 12 servers' DRAM over RDMA/CXL, with reconstruction on failure done by a NIC-offloaded decoder.
why: Replication overhead drops from 3.0x to 1.2x, so replicated in-memory tiers need ~2.5x less DRAM at the cost of ~5-20 us degraded-read latency (cost/bit, capital).

title: Swap per-request RAG prefill for shared position-independent chunk KV
idea: Substitute per-request KV with a shared library of chunk KV. Each popular retrieval chunk is prefilled once at position zero; at use, its RoPE keys are re-rotated to the real offset and only the first ~5% boundary tokens are recomputed to restore cross-chunk attention, so concurrent requests reference one copy. No memory interface change.
why: RAG serving duplicates the same document KV across users. Sharing it cuts KV footprint 3-10x for popular corpora and saves prefill compute.

title: Swap roles: GPU does matmul, CPU DDR hosts attention
idea: Rearrange the accelerator split: the GPU keeps only the weights and runs the dense GEMMs, while the KV cache and the memory-bound attention move to CPU-side DDR5 with CPU or near-memory attention kernels, exchanging small per-token vectors.
why: HBM costs ~3x the wafer area per bit of DDR5 (fact 6); moving KV (often >50% of serving memory) to DDR cuts DRAM wafer area per served token ~2x.

title: Quarry-side crushing: filter data in storage before it reaches DRAM
idea: Quarries crush ore at the pit so they ship less tonnage. Predicates, projections, decompression and vector-similarity prefiltering are pushed into SSD and CXL controllers (computational storage), so the DRAM buffer pool holds only qualifying rows or vectors instead of whole pages.
why: Databases and vector search provision buffer pools at 5-10x the useful data; pushdown cuts buffer-pool DRAM 3-10x for scan-heavy and ANN workloads.

title: Colander: learned index models replace in-memory B-trees
idea: A colander keeps only what matters: replace database and key-value indexes with piecewise-linear learned models plus small error buffers, evaluated by a tiny controller-side unit, so index structures shrink from GBs to MBs.
why: Indexes are often 20-50% of in-memory database DRAM; 10-100x index compression.

title: CDC 6600 Extended Core Storage rebuilt on fully depreciated DRAM fabs
idea: Revive ECS, the CDC 6600's huge, slower, block-transfer-only memory: build a wide (1-4 KB block), ~1 us bulk tier from 2x-nm-era DRAM lines whose tools are fully depreciated, reached only by a block-copy instruction with no load/store and no coherence. Compilers and runtimes explicitly stage tiles from ECS into a much smaller fast DDR5/HBM.
why: Fact 4 (depreciation ~55% of wafer cost): zero-depreciation old-node bits with relaxed timing approach leading-edge cost per bit without EUV; keeping only the hot 20-30% in fast DRAM roughly halves premium DRAM demand.

title: Swap idle consumer RAM into a paid cold-cache donation network
idea: Substitute data-center cache DRAM with idle installed RAM. A client app rents a revocable, encrypted, erasure-coded slice of idle PC and console RAM to a CDN-style tier for cold, latency-tolerant objects, and pays owners in credits.
why: Raises usable supply without fabs: 1 GB on each of 50M devices is 50 PB of cache, which offloads warm-cache tiers in data centers.

title: Capsule wardrobe weights: one global codebook for every layer
idea: A capsule wardrobe mixes a few garments into many outfits; store one model-wide codebook of 64K 8-dim weight vectors in on-chip SRAM and represent every layer as 16-bit indices into it (2 bits/weight), trained with codebook-aware fine-tuning.
why: 2 bits/weight with a shared on-chip codebook avoids per-layer codebook overhead; ~8x smaller weights in DRAM vs FP16.

title: Magnify thread count 1000x so flash serves as main memory
idea: Magnify hardware contexts to thousands per core (barrel processor) so the core tolerates ~2-5 us line reads from low-latency NAND used as load/store main memory. DRAM shrinks to a 1/10-size line buffer.
why: Throughput workloads (graph, analytics, serving) get 10-20x capacity per dollar, because flash costs ~1/10-1/20 of DRAM per bit.

title: Postal ZIP codes: region-relative 32-bit pointers in hardware
idea: Borrowed from postal routing (zone plus local address): an ISA extension where pointers are 32-bit 'ZIP + offset' values resolved through a region register file in the load unit, letting native data structures use half-size pointers, not just JVM compressed oops.
why: Pointer-heavy data (graphs, trees, object heaps) is 30-50% pointers; 20-35% footprint reduction across native code.

title: Fleet-trained shared dictionaries for memory page compression
idea: Combine zstd-style trained dictionaries with a mature-node CXL memory-compression controller: the operator trains dictionaries offline on sampled page contents per workload class, loads them into controller SRAM, and tags each compressed page with its dictionary ID.
why: Shared dictionaries roughly double ratios on small 4 KB pages (about 2x to 3-4x), so a mature-node controller over older DRAM delivers more effective capacity than raw EUV parts.

title: HMC logic layer, fixed: KV vector-quantization codec in HBM base die
idea: Hybrid Memory Cube put logic under DRAM but died with no killer function and proprietary SerDes. Give the HBM4 custom base die one job: a vector-quantization codec that stores KV blocks as per-layer codebook indices plus small residuals and expands them on read, with codebooks held in base-die SRAM.
why: 2-4x more KV per HBM stack without GPU kernel changes, attacking HBM's ~3x area-per-bit tax.

title: Ad-tech cardinality extreme: sketch-first databases that answer approximately
idea: From ad platforms counting billions of distinct users: in-memory analytics keep HyperLogLog, KLL quantile and count-min sketches as the primary resident structures and push exact rows to flash, answering dashboards from sketches and touching rows only for audits.
why: Sketches are 100-1000x smaller than raw rows for aggregate queries; resident DRAM falls 10x+ with a matching water cut.

title: Binaries ship heap-trained compression dictionaries loaded at context switch
idea: TRIZ #10 Prior action: at build/profile time, train a 4-16 KB dictionary on representative heap snapshots of each application and embed it in the ELF; the OS loads it into a dictionary slot in the memory controller on context switch, so line-granular compression is application-specific from the first write.
why: Generic line compressors reach ~1.3-1.6x; app-trained dictionaries give 2-3x on structured heaps (protobufs, JSON, strings).

title: Salamander regeneration: rewritable row remapping that never runs out
idea: One-time fuse-based post-package repair is replaced by a rewritable on-module remap SRAM plus spare rows reserved per bank, so as cells weaken with age the module regrows healthy rows indefinitely and recycled chips are re-repaired at every life cycle.
why: Lifetime and reuse yield: second-life DRAM usable at 95%+ capacity instead of being binned out.

title: Benetton postponement: dye per-tenant fine-tunes at compute time
idea: Benetton knits undyed sweaters and dyes them at the last moment. One base model stays resident and serves thousands of fine-tuned variants. Each variant is stored as a 1-bit sign delta plus per-row scales (or a low-rank adapter), and the 'dye' is fused into the GEMM, so no variant is ever materialized in DRAM.
why: N full model copies become one base plus N deltas of about 1/16 the size, a 10-100x memory reduction for multi-tenant fine-tune hosting.

title: Straintronic nanomagnets compute bitmap-index logic in place
idea: Store database and feature bitmaps as Galfenol nanomagnet states on an AlN piezo layer. A voltage-induced strain pulse rotates the magnets, and dipole coupling between neighbors computes AND/OR across bit-columns in place, so compressed bitmap indexes are queried without decompressing into DRAM. Galfenol's ~670 C Curie point and shape anisotropy keep the energy barrier above 60 kT at 125 C.
why: Analytics indexes stay compressed and are computed in place, with 5-10x less DRAM for in-vehicle map and feature queries and aJ-scale switching.

title: Overlapping reading frames share MSB bit-planes between correlated tensors
idea: Viruses read one RNA in shifted frames to make different proteins; a base model and its fine-tunes (or strongly correlated projections) store a shared most-significant bit-plane once, each variant keeping only its own low-order planes, read through frame-specific offsets.
why: Capacity: 30-50% savings for families of correlated weights.

title: Hollow-core fiber widens memory-pooling radius by 45 percent
idea: Remote-memory latency is bounded by the speed of light in the medium: ~5 ns/m in solid glass, ~3.4 ns/m in hollow-core fiber. Wire memory pools with hollow-core fiber so a 300 ns round-trip budget reaches ~47% farther, roughly doubling the floor area, and so the number of servers, that one pool can cover.
why: Pool headroom scales roughly as 1/sqrt(N), so doubling the servers per pool trims another ~5-10% of provisioned DRAM.

title: Beach metal detector: back-end capacitive key-sketch array picks tokens
idea: Sweep a detector before digging: keep 1-bit sketches of all keys in a back-end HZO/MIM capacitive compute-in-memory array (crystallized <=400 C) on the accelerator; a query is broadcast as charge, the array returns top-k token indices in one shot, and only those full K/V blocks are fetched from a cheap CXL/flash tier.
why: Full KV leaves HBM entirely (10-50x less DRAM for long context) because only ~1-5% of tokens are fetched per step.

title: Artist's negative space: VM pages stored as diffs against rack-golden images
idea: Painters define a shape by what is missing. One golden copy of each common OS and runtime image lives in rack-shared CXL memory. Each VM page is stored as a sparse XOR or byte-diff delta against its matching golden page, found by content hash at boot and by background scanning.
why: VMs share 70-90% near-identical pages that differ by a few bytes, which exact dedup misses. Delta storage reclaims 15-30% of host DRAM in VM-dense racks.

title: Predictive-coding memory: residuals in DRAM, predictor in SRAM
idea: Reverse the roles of data and model: a small predictor (e.g. a linear map from layer L-1 KV to layer L KV, or a neighbor-line delta model) lives in on-chip SRAM, and DRAM stores only the quantized residual between prediction and truth; the controller adds prediction and residual back together on read.
why: KV caches and embedding tables are strongly correlated across layers and neighbors, so residuals need 2-4 bits instead of 16: ~3-5x effective capacity on the largest AI memory consumers.

title: Jacquard cards: KV vectors replaced by shared punch-card codes
idea: A Jacquard loom weaves endless patterns from a small deck of punch cards. Here each attention head keeps a learned deck of 4,096 KV 'cards' (a product-quantization codebook of about 1 MB, pinned in SRAM) shared by every user, and the KV cache stores only 12-bit card indices per sub-vector. The attention kernel computes q-dot-card once per card, then gathers scores by index.
why: KV cache memory shrinks 8-16x, and lookup-table attention is also faster, which frees the HBM capacity that limits batch size and context length.

title: Match-line metal mask makes one subarray per bank a fingerprint CAM
idea: One added metal mask lays wired-OR match lines across a dedicated subarray in each bank that stores 32-bit line fingerprints. A search broadcasts a fingerprint on the bitlines, and every matching row asserts its match line in one ~20 ns cycle. That makes 64 B dedup lookups possible inside DRAM without a CPU hash table.
why: Line-level dedup finds 1.3-2x more duplicates than page-level dedup but was impractical because of index-lookup cost. The in-DRAM CAM removes that cost.

title: Cascade router sends easy queries to small models first
idea: IFR: every query is answered with the smallest memory possible. Closest with no hardware: a confidence-calibrated cascade routes queries to a 3B model (6 GB) first and escalates to the 400B model only when a verifier flags uncertainty, so fewer replicas of the giant model are needed.
why: If 70% of traffic stays small, giant-model replicas and their HBM drop ~3x.

title: Hardware video encoders compress parked KV caches as 10-bit frames
idea: Box: lossy compression × existing GPU video engines × per-head KV tensor × session parked × HEVC 10-bit with channel-reordered frames. Parked KV caches are reordered so tokens become frame time and channels become pixels, then encoded by idle on-die video engines and decoded on resume.
why: If token-to-token correlation holds, parked KV shrinks 5–10× using fixed-function engines already shipped; no new silicon, no fluorinated chemistry.

title: Back-EMF flush: fan and PSU inertia power the persistence dump
idea: As hard drives use spindle back-EMF to park heads on power loss, harvest the rotational energy of server fans (~10-15 J each) and PSU bulk capacitors through a boost converter to flush a bounded dirty set from DRAM to on-board NAND (~3 J per GB).
why: Makes DRAM-as-cache-over-flash power-safe without batteries or supercaps, so DRAM can shrink to a dirty-bounded cache over cheap persistent flash.

title: Joule-and-dollar ledger deciding store versus recompute per tensor
idea: Price every resident object by its physical rent: capacity amortization ($/GB-s) plus refresh energy (~46 fJ/bit per 64 ms), against the energy and time to rebuild it from its inputs (FLOPs x ~0.5 pJ). A runtime keeps a lineage graph, like Spark or autograd, and drops any tensor, query intermediate or memo entry whose rebuild cost is below its rent, extending activation checkpointing to all data.
why: 30-60% smaller footprint for training activations, analytics intermediates and memo caches, because energy per FLOP has fallen ~10x faster than DRAM cost per bit.

title: Memory-first chassis: DIMMs outlive three CPU generations
idea: Reverse which part is disposable: servers are built around a 10-year memory backplane (CXL-attached DIMM sleds), and the CPU and accelerator boards become the modules swapped every 3 years, so DRAM is never retired along with the server.
why: Fleet DRAM purchases fall roughly 2-3x over a decade, and the reused bits need no new neon-litho or helium-dependent wafers.

title: On-sensor tokenizers so raw frames never land in DRAM
idea: IFR: perception data enters memory already understood. Closest in plain Si CMOS: stacked image sensors with a small patch-embedding network in the logic layer emit compact tokens or event deltas instead of raw frames, so camera pipelines skip multi-frame DRAM buffers.
why: Cuts frame-buffer DRAM 10-50x in phones, cars and robots, and removes the matching DRAM traffic.

title: Rebar concrete: protected outlier rebar, bulk codes in 1%-BER cells
idea: Reinforced concrete puts steel only where strength is needed. Weights and KV are split into a sparse 'rebar' of outliers plus all scale factors, kept in a small strongly-ECC'd region (about 3% of bits), and a dense 'concrete' of 3-4-bit codes stored raw in 1%-BER cells. With outliers removed and codes clamped to a narrow range, any flip moves a value by at most one bounded code range, which is a tiny perturbation in a dot product.
why: About 97% of model bits move into cheap, unrefreshed or defect-tolerant cells while also being quantized 4x, so the high-grade DRAM needed for weights drops about 10x.

title: 32-bit relative pointers ABI shrinks C/C++ heaps
idea: Reverse the 64-bit default: an allocator ABI puts each process's heap in 4 GB regions and the compiler stores pointers as 32-bit offsets from a region base register (as Java compressed oops and V8 already do), using fat pointers only where regions are crossed.
why: Pointer-heavy data structures shrink 25-40%, recovering DRAM through a recompile of software on existing CPUs.

title: Expert-major MoE serving: tokens queue, experts load once per wave
idea: Rearrange MoE serving from token-major to expert-major: tokens routed to cold experts wait in per-expert queues, and each expert's weights stream from flash once per wave to process its whole queue, so only hot experts stay in DRAM.
why: Most experts sit idle at any instant; resident expert weights shrink 3-8x for a bounded rise in latency.

title: Retail UPC registry: global value interning in the memory controller
idea: Borrowed from UPC barcodes, where one global registry gives each product a short code: the memory controller learns a table of the ~4K most frequent 64-bit values (pointer prefixes, enum constants, common floats) and stores them as 12-bit codes inside a compressed line format shared across all processes.
why: Value locality in real heaps is high; 1.3-1.8x effective capacity, complementary to zero elision and dedup.

title: All-SRAM American inference box: zero DRAM, logic-fab memory only
idea: Po: memory made only of logic transistors. Intel 18A (AZ/OR) SRAM chiplets hybrid-bonded 8-high with Foveros Direct in Rio Rancho (NM) hold a 4-bit entropy-coded model whose attention/state-space hybrid design has fixed-size recurrent state, so KV never grows and no DRAM is needed.
why: Sidesteps the lack of leading-edge U.S. DRAM by using U.S. logic capacity that exists; fits inference in ~10-40 GB of SRAM and slashes data-movement energy (fact 5).

title: Barium getter: co-accessed objects gathered into one mini-row
idea: A barium getter pulls stray gas molecules onto one surface; a profile-guided placement pass co-locates objects that are accessed together into the same 512 B mini-row of a DRAM with subarray-level partial activation, so a pointer chase opens 1/16 of a page instead of a full 8 KB row.
why: Attacks the 128x overfetch: random reads drop from ~5.9 pJ per useful bit toward ~0.5 pJ (about 10x), and lower bandwidth demand lets bandwidth-provisioned systems buy fewer DRAM channels (energy, cost/bit).

title: Bubble memory, fixed: magnetic loop memory for sequentially-read KV
idea: Magnetic bubble memory (TI, Intel Magnetics) died on millisecond serial access through major/minor loops. Attention reads all K/V in order every decode step, so store KV in domain-wall racetrack loops that shift continuously in lockstep with the token loop, re-synced every lap by a marker domain so positioning errors never accumulate.
why: Capacitorless, transistor-sparse, refresh-free KV storage at potentially <4F^2/bit for the largest inference memory consumer.

title: Event-sourced memory rebuilt by deterministic replay
idea: Worsen: keep every intermediate state of a long computation resident. Flip: store periodic checkpoints and the input log on cheap storage, and rebuild any needed state by deterministic replay on cheap cores, with DRAM holding only the live frontier.
why: Cost: state that is 100x larger than its log costs storage prices, not DRAM prices; trades recompute time.

title: Swap declared field widths for profile-narrowed fields with overflow escape
idea: Substitute programmer-declared widths with observed widths. A profile-guided compiler pass finds struct fields and arrays whose values fit fewer bits (64-bit ints below 2^16, integral doubles), re-lays them narrow with hot/cold structure splitting, and adds an escape bit that boxes rare outliers into a side table.
why: Data-heavy C/C++/Rust services often waste 30-50% of struct bytes, so heaps shrink 1.3-1.8x on unchanged DDR.

title: Fuzzy structures: compiler swaps exact maps for sketches when allowed
idea: Po: memory is approximate by default. Developers annotate tolerances (e.g., count within 1%), and the compiler/runtime substitutes count-min sketches, HyperLogLog, quotient or Bloom filters for exact hash maps and sets in telemetry, dedup and analytics code.
why: Replaces GB-scale exact counters with MB-scale sketches: 100-1000x memory reduction for those structures.

title: Zygote fork: preinitialize runtimes once, copy-on-write everywhere
idea: Inverts 'each container boots its own runtime': as with Android's zygote, each node keeps a pre-warmed Python/JVM/ML-framework process with libraries and shared weights loaded, and every new container forks from it and shares pages copy-on-write. Software only, on installed servers.
why: Per-instance memory for interpreter, libraries and shared weights (often 200 MB-2 GB) is paid once per node, cutting container fleet DRAM 2-4x.

title: Printed analog count-min sketch tags summarize at the sensor
idea: Constraint (printable/roll-to-roll): printed sensor tags accumulate events into a handful of printed capacitor 'buckets' selected by printed hash wiring, forming an analog count-min sketch or histogram. Each interval the gateway reads a 64-value summary instead of buffering raw event streams in server DRAM.
why: IoT ingestion clusters keep raw streams in DRAM for windowed aggregation; pre-aggregating at the sensor cuts ingest memory 10-100x for aggregate analytics.

title: Zygote fleets: every microVM is a copy-on-write clone
idea: Po: every program is a clone of one ancestor. Serverless and microservice fleets on U.S.-built servers boot one golden, fully warmed microVM per runtime and fork every instance from it copy-on-write, Android-zygote style at VM scale, so warm pools share runtime, JIT code and heap prefixes.
why: Warm-pool memory is mostly identical runtime state; CoW forking cuts per-instance resident memory 3-10x, stretching scarce domestic DRAM.

title: Mercury-delay-line weight carousel shared by a whole rack
idea: Like a mercury delay line, where data recirculates and any tap reads it as it passes, one copy of the model weights streams continuously from a single dense store around an optical WDM ring that passes every accelerator in a rack. Each accelerator forms its batch, multiplies the weights as they fly by and waits for the next revolution, keeping only KV cache and activations locally.
why: Capacity: replaces N per-accelerator weight copies with one per rack (8-64x less weight HBM/DRAM); a 70 GB model on a 10 Tb/s ring revolves every ~56 ms, inside decode-step budgets for throughput serving.

title: Eliminate the zero-defect requirement: DIMMs from downgraded DRAM dies
idea: Buy DRAM dies that failed full-spec binning, assemble them into modules at a contract manufacturer with an on-module SPD map of bad rows, and have a Linux memmap/badram driver retire those pages at boot.
why: Recovers supply that fabs scrap or sell for scrap, at deep discount: 5-15% more usable bits from existing wafer output.

title: Hot-line compaction packs hot 64-byte lines from many pages
idea: Inverts 'the 4 KB page is the unit of placement': the memory controller tracks hotness per 64 B line and migrates hot lines from many sparse pages into dense DRAM 'hot pages' through a line-remap table, leaving the cold remainder of each page in CXL or flash tiers.
why: Typical pages have only 10-25% hot lines, so page-granular tiering wastes the rest; line-granular placement cuts the DRAM needed for the same hit rate 2-3x.

title: Reed–Solomon striping replaces triple replication in in-memory stores
idea: Box: redundancy reduction × distributed key-value tier × object stripe × on write × RS(6,3) with NIC offload. Objects are striped across nodes with parity encoded by the NIC; reads gather data fragments in parallel over RDMA, with decode only on failure.
why: Durability overhead drops from 3× to 1.5×, halving DRAM for replicated caches and session stores fleetwide.

title: Eliminate fork's 2x memory peak with userfaultfd write-protect snapshots
idea: A 10-person team ships a library that replaces fork-based snapshots (Redis BGSAVE, Postgres-style checkpoints) with userfaultfd write-protection: the snapshotter streams pages to disk and copies only pages written mid-snapshot.
why: In-memory stores are provisioned at about 2x their data to survive fork copy-on-write storms; removing that cuts their DRAM by up to 45%.

title: Garbage collector living inside the memory expander
idea: Inverts 'GC is a host-CPU job that needs 2-3x heap headroom': a CXL Type-3 expander runs a concurrent copying/compacting collector next to its DRAM, with hardware forwarding pointers serving as the read barrier. Because it compacts continuously, managed heaps run at 1.1-1.3x live data.
why: Java/Go/.NET fleets reserve large heap headroom; shrinking it frees 30-50% of the DRAM those services occupy.

title: Key-only residency: values fetched from flash for top-k tokens
idea: TRIZ #16 Partial action: keep only the quantized keys of long contexts in HBM, because keys decide where attention goes, and leave values on NVMe/CXL; after scoring, fetch values only for the top-k attended tokens (typically 1-5%) with batched reads.
why: Values are half the KV footprint and sparse attention touches few of them; ~2x KV HBM reduction with bounded flash bandwidth.

title: Bit-plane layout: MSB planes in DRAM, LSB planes in flash
idea: Rearrange tensors from word-major to bit-plane-major: the top 3-4 bit planes stay in DRAM and the lower planes live in flash or CXL memory, fetched only when a per-layer confidence monitor (e.g. logit margin) asks for more precision.
why: Most inference steps need only the MSB planes: ~2x effective DRAM capacity and bandwidth for weights and activations, with precision added on demand.

title: Follow-the-night memory: shift DRAM-heavy work to wherever it's cold
idea: From polar stations that schedule heavy work into the cold dark: a global scheduler migrates DRAM-heavy batch jobs, with CXL-flash snapshots of their memory, to whichever region is currently in cold night, so each region's DRAM serves local interactive load by day and global batch load by night, always on dry or free-air cooling.
why: One DRAM pool serves two workloads (~2x fewer bits), and running memory-heavy work only in cold ambient lets sites drop evaporative cooling, cutting water >10x.

title: Hardware interning engine stores each string or record once
idea: IFR: every distinct value exists once. Closest with mature-node Al/Ti logic: a memory-side engine hash-conses immutable strings, JSON nodes and tuples at allocation, returning a refcounted handle to an existing copy, with 64-bit hash probes done near memory.
why: String and record duplication is 10-30% of heap in web, log and analytics services.

title: DIMM data-buffer chip doubles as a base-delta decompressor
idea: Combine the MRDIMM/LRDIMM data-buffer and RCD chips (already made on 28-40 nm DUV processes) with a base-delta-immediate compression engine and a small remap table, so a DIMM built from older 1y/1z DUV DRAM dies presents ~1.6-2x its raw capacity to the host.
why: Lets non-EUV DRAM nodes match EUV-node logical density per module, skipping the 5-7 EUV layers (fact 4) while all added logic stays on mature, U.S.-available nodes.

title: Soviet-style socialist competition: bounties for memory-footprint patches
idea: Like a five-year-plan competition, but paid. A $600k bounty pool pays per verified GB saved on standard benchmarks of the 50 most-deployed open-source infrastructure packages (Postgres, Redis, Kafka, Elasticsearch, PyTorch DataLoader, Chromium). A $400k CI harness measures peak and steady RSS before and after each merged patch.
why: Code that runs on millions of servers multiplies every saving: a 10% footprint cut in these packages frees millions of GB globally, which may be the highest-leverage use of $1M.

title: Hermit-crab vacancy chains cascade memory through fleet tiers
idea: Hermit crabs line up by size and swap shells in a chain when a large new shell appears; a fleet protocol makes every new HBM or DDR5 purchase trigger a planned cascade (training, inference, CXL pool, edge, recycler) with standardized sleds and internal transfer prices at each step.
why: Supply strategy: average bit lifetime from ~4 to 8-10 years, roughly halving new-bit demand for equal capacity.

title: Diablo Memory1 lesson: royalty-free patent pool for memory tiering
idea: Diablo's Memory1 (flash on a DIMM used as memory) died largely from a Netlist patent suit and single-platform qualification. Form a defensive, royalty-free OIN-style patent pool covering flash/CXL memory tiering, page promotion and DIMM buffering so tiering vendors and hyperscalers can ship without existential lawsuit risk.
why: Removes the legal risk that killed tiered-memory products, accelerating adoption of 2-5x cheaper capacity tiers.

title: Parent reading food labels: memory-footprint labels in software procurement
idea: Parents compare nutrition labels. An open 'Memory Facts' label (peak RSS, steady-state RSS per 1k users, bytes per stored record) is measured by a reference harness, and the campaign gets federal and large-enterprise procurement (GSA, state CIOs) to require it, as Energy Star did for power. Costs: standards work, the harness and outreach.
why: Buyer pressure pushes memory efficiency across the software supply chain, and 5-10% footprint cuts per procurement cycle compound.

title: Lichen pairing turns retired servers into RDMA memory donors
idea: Lichen fuses a fungus and an alga into a new organism; a stripped retired server (old CPU, full DRAM) runs a tiny memory-server OS and lends its DRAM over RDMA as remote swap to new servers, its only job being memory.
why: Supply: retiring servers' DRAM gets a second 3-5-year life; 25-40% less new DRAM per new server.

title: Learned index replaces the SSD's flash-translation DRAM
idea: Combine learned index structures (piecewise-linear models over sorted keys) with the SSD flash translation layer: because FTL writes are mostly sequential within streams, a few MB of linear segments plus a small exception table map LBAs to flash pages instead of a 4-byte-per-4KB page table held in DRAM.
why: Enterprise SSDs carry ~1 GB of DRAM per TB; a 50-100x smaller map returns a noticeable slice of global DRAM bit demand to host use.

title: Williams-tube leaky charge stores optimizer momentum without refresh
idea: Williams tubes lost charge and needed regeneration; here decay is the feature: momentum/Adam moment buffers live as analog charge on a university-built capacitor array whose leakage time constant is tuned to the beta decay per step, so physics performs the exponential moving average with no refresh and no digital storage.
why: Optimizer states are ~8 of 16 bytes per parameter in mixed-precision training; replacing them with leaky analog cells roughly halves training memory.
